Overview At SAIC Volkswagen, I developed an active-learning framework for automotive aerodynamic performance prediction. It combined machine-learning models with CFD so that uncertain predictions could lead to new high-fidelity calculations and model updates.
The problem A prediction model can provide a quick estimate, but its reliability depends on how well a new design resembles the available training data. The framework needed a way to identify cases requiring more simulation evidence.
Framework The workflow combines MLP and GNN models with CFD and wind-tunnel information. It connects a design-stage prediction process to a training system that incorporates additional data.
Design stages, confidence checks, and the training loop in the aerodynamic prediction framework.
My contribution I trained the GNN network, and built the active-learning GNN–CFD workflow. Low-confidence predictions triggered high-fidelity CFD calculations, and the resulting data entered subsequent model retraining.

Overview As a CFD Methodology Engineer at SAIC Volkswagen, I developed and calibrated automated OpenFOAM workflows for external and underhood aerodynamics.
Methodology work A vehicle simulation needs more than a converged solver run. Mesh resolution and numerical settings affect the result, and automated workflows must remain reliable across complex geometries.
My work included mesh-sensitivity studies, convergence assessment, and numerical robustness checks. These checks supported the use of a consistent simulation methodology across automotive cases.
My contribution Established and calibrated automated OpenFOAM simulation workflows. Assessed mesh sensitivity and convergence for external and underhood vehicle flows. Investigated numerical robustness on complex automotive geometries. Mentored graduate engineers in OpenFOAM, parallel computing, and machine learning. Connected projects This methodology work accompanied my development of SPH models for water management, an active-learning aerodynamic prediction framework, and aeroacoustic noise-prediction software.

Overview My MSc project at Imperial College London studied gyrotactic swimming microorganisms in a vertical pipe. Gravity and shear affect their swimming direction, while the cells also influence the flow through buoyancy. This coupling can produce nonuniform concentration profiles and bifurcations.
I worked under the supervision of Prof. Yongyun Hwang and Lloyd Fung.
Gyrotactic cell distributions in upward and downward pipe flow.
Numerical model I developed an unsteady finite-volume solver in MATLAB for the coupled cell-conservation and momentum equations. The implementation used a semi-implicit first-order scheme for cell conservation and an implicit scheme for momentum.
The study considered fixed flow rate, prescribed pressure gradient, and time-periodic pressure forcing. Conservation and boundary conditions mattered when comparing behavior across different flow directions and initial conditions.
Coupled cell-conservation and momentum equations.
Bifurcation analysis At fixed flow rate, the calculations reproduced a bifurcation at a Richardson number of 8 and showed a qualitative match near 25 with the reference results discussed in my thesis.
Centerline concentration under fixed-flow-rate conditions.
For prescribed pressure gradients, I examined how the initial flow rate affected the final concentration and velocity profiles. Some cases exhibited an interval of divergence before convergence, whose extent depended on the forcing and initial condition.
Download video Time evolution of concentration and velocity for different initial conditions. Oscillatory forcing I also derived a linearized state-space system to study the response to sinusoidal pressure gradients and investigated how the parameters affected its frequency response.
Centerline-velocity frequency response to periodic pressure forcing.
Report and background Read my MSc report.
Background literature: Fung, L., Bearon, R. N., and Hwang, Y. (2020). Bifurcation and stability of downflowing gyrotactic micro-organism suspensions in a vertical pipe. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 902, A26. DOI: 10.1017/jfm.2020.614.

The problem Aerodynamic optimization needs gradients that tell us how a change in shape affects a quantity such as drag. Conventional adjoint calculations become difficult when a flow exhibits chaotic dynamics, particularly when the objective depends on a long-time average.
Least Squares Shadowing offers a way to calculate sensitivities in this setting. Its storage and computational requirements are a major obstacle for industrial CFD.
My research I work on shadowing-based sensitivity analysis and adjoint methods in OpenFOAM. The research programme includes reformulating the shadowing problem and investigating iterative solution methods and data compression to reduce its cost. The intended application is aerodynamic shape optimization around bluff bodies and automotive geometries.
This is ongoing doctoral research. The image below illustrates the automotive application.
Automotive flow visualization illustrating the application. This is not a completed result from my PhD.

Overview I coupled the FEBio finite-element structural solver with an in-house immersed-boundary CFD solver for large-deformation fluid–structure interaction at Vanderbilt University.
The two solvers address different parts of the problem. FEBio handles tissue mechanics, while the immersed-boundary solver handles the flow around a moving structure. The coupling exchanges fluid loads and structural motion during the simulation.
Solver coupling The flowchart below shows the exchange of interface pressures or tractions, nodal positions, and velocities. Each solver advances its own equations, and the interface iteration checks convergence before completing the time step.
Exchange of fluid loads and structural motion within a coupled time step.
Biological application The APS conference abstract describes validation against FSI benchmarks and application to bioprosthetic heart valves with nonlinear, hyperelastic, and anisotropic tissue behavior. The study examined pressure gradients, valve-surface pressures, effective orifice area, and flow patterns.
Flow-induced deformation of the valve leaflets.
My contribution My work focused on integrating the structural and fluid frameworks for biomedical FSI. The wider collaboration included computational assessment of prosthetic aortic valve designs with California Medical Innovations Institute and Prima Medical Technologies GmbH.
Presentation Sarkar, N., Li, S., and Luo, H. (2025). A coupled FEBio–immersed boundary framework for fluid-structure interaction in biological applications. 78th Annual Meeting of the APS Division of Fluid Dynamics, Houston, TX. Conference abstract.

Overview I carried out my undergraduate thesis at Universidad Politécnica de Madrid through an Erasmus+ exchange from Northwestern Polytechnical University. The work combined the DLR-TAU flow solver with BiGlobal stability analysis to examine unstable flow behavior.
My supervisors were Prof. Eusebio Valero Sanchez and Prof. Yaguo Lyu.
Cylinder validation I first used cylinder flow at a Reynolds number of 60 to check the flow calculation and stability analysis. The Strouhal number agreed with the experimental reference in the thesis, and the analysis extracted the dominant mode of the wake.
Eigenvalue spectrum and dominant mode for the cylinder validation case.
Airfoil separation For the NACA0012 airfoil, I calculated cases across angles of attack from 0° to 19°. In the conditions studied, the separation threshold occurred at 18.9°. Unsteady simulation and frequency analysis supported the extraction and visualization of the dominant instability mode.
Eigenvalue spectrum and dominant velocity mode for the airfoil.
Erasmus+ supported the undergraduate thesis exchange.

Overview I extended DualSPHysics, an open-source smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) solver, in C++/CUDA. The project introduced surface-tension and aerodynamic-drag effects for GPU-accelerated automotive rainwater simulations.
The work formed part of a collaboration between SAIC Volkswagen and Northwestern Polytechnical University. I led a team of four, working on model implementation and code structure, with academic supervision from Prof. Zhe Ji.
Engineering problem Rainwater can travel along a vehicle surface and enter areas where it causes an unwanted experience. One example is opening a wet trunk after rainfall. Predicting this motion helps engineers assess water-management behavior during design.
Water trajectories over the vehicle body.
Aerodynamic drag The air-drag extension enabled one-way air–water coupling. The implementation calculates particle drag using the exposed area and the local flow information. The algorithm includes a treatment of occluded area when estimating the area exposed to the surrounding air.
Particle drag calculation, including exposed area and occlusion.
The comparisons below examine the effect of including air drag in a falling droplet and an injected water jet.
Droplet velocity and terminal-velocity comparison. Water-jet trajectories with and without air drag.
Surface tension and wetting I also implemented surface-tension effects and calibrated contact angles using a droplet-on-plate case. These tests check the wetting behavior before applying the model to a vehicle surface.
60° contact angle 90° contact angle 120° contact angle Water movement on the trunk surface during opening.
Methods DualSPHysics, C++, CUDA, SPH, surface tension, wetting, and particle drag. The figures document the implementation and its test cases.

Overview I developed the algorithm and graphical interface for Automotive Aeroacoustic Noise Prediction Software (WNPS) at SAIC Volkswagen. The software predicts the wind noise propagation paths of the holes & gaps and provides guidance for the development of wind noise performance on the early stage.
Physics-informed Neural Network (PINN) and data science techniques are adopted to analyze experimental data and predict.
Prediction task The software reads vehicle information and experimental configurations and predicts an Articulation Index, a measure of speech intelligibility in noise. Engineers can compare the output across test states to study how changes to sealing strips affect wind-noise performance.
The interface brings vehicle data, model inputs, and predicted results into one workflow. Its comparison plots make it easier to inspect the effect of different experimental configurations.
The prediction interface, with annotated input and output panels.
My contribution I was the primary developer for the prediction algorithm, deployment, and GUI, and managed a team of three. The implementation used Python, PyTorch, and PyQt.
Project material WNPS user’s guide
Software manual (Chinese).

Overview At Vanderbilt University, I worked on CT-based geometry reconstruction and finite-element simulation of the upper airway. The project studied how ansa cervicalis stimulation (ACS) changes airway anatomy in the context of obstructive sleep apnea. I am a joint first author of the resulting paper.
Modeling approach The study reconstructed anatomy from one adult head-and-neck CT. The workflow combined segmentation, surface smoothing, tetrahedral meshing, and registration of the anatomical components. It used literature-based linear elastic tissue properties.
The model represented ACS as a downward load on the thyroid cartilage and inspiratory loading as a −70 Pa pressure on the airway lumen. Tissue displacement and airway area provided the comparison between loading conditions. Published study.
Anatomical segmentation used to construct the finite-element model. Figure 1 from Gupta et al. (2026).
Results The simulations showed coordinated downward motion of the hyolaryngeal structures and reduced airway narrowing under negative pressure. Epiglottic displacement decreased from 5.0 to 2.2 mm, while retropalatal area increased from 16.98 to 20.43 mm².
These are findings from a single-subject proof-of-concept model. They support investigation of the mechanism rather than a population-level prediction of treatment response. Results and limitations.
Negative-pressure loading without ACS (A, B) and with ACS (C, D). Figure 6 from Gupta et al. (2026).
Publication Gupta, M., Li, S., Luo, H., Kent, D. T., and Li, Y. (2026). Finite Element Analysis of Upper Airway in Ansa Cervicalis Stimulation for Obstructive Sleep Apnea. The Laryngoscope, 136(10), 4575–4584. DOI: 10.1002/lary.70603.
Mukund Gupta and Songrui Li contributed equally as joint first authors.

I am an MSCA Doctoral Candidate in the Parallel CFD & Optimization Unit at the National Technical University of Athens. Within the FairCFD Doctoral Network, I develop shadowing-based sensitivity and adjoint methods for chaotic flows, with applications to automotive aerodynamic optimization in collaboration with Toyota Gazoo Racing. After completing my MSc at Imperial College London, I spent three years at SAIC Volkswagen working on automotive CFD and scientific machine learning. I then joined Vanderbilt University to study fluid–structure interaction in biomedical applications. I now work with the team behind OpenFOAM’s adjointShapeOptimizationFoam, extending my focus to sensitivity analysis and optimization for complex engineering flows.
Alongside this work, I explore how Scientific Machine Learning and AI-assisted workflows can improve our understanding of nonlinear flow dynamics and support efficient, physically consistent simulations.

CFD and nonlinear dynamical systems overlap with LLM and deep learning, automotive flow and optimization, and bio flow and patient-specific modeling. The biomedical overlap is FSI.
